notes.summary: A random variable gives a number to each outcome of an experiment. Paper 2 asks you to work with probability mass and density functions, find expectation and variance, and use the standard distributions: binomial, Poisson, geometric, negative binomial and hypergeometric (discrete) and uniform, exponential and normal (continuous). Know each distribution's formula, mean, variance and special properties.

concepts.title: Random variables
concepts.body:
• A random variable X is a rule that gives a real number to each outcome. Toss 2 coins and let X = number of heads: X takes 0, 1 or 2.
  • Discrete: takes countable values (0, 1, 2, …). Described by a probability mass function (pmf) p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σp(x) = 1.
  • Continuous: takes any value in an interval. Described by a probability density function (pdf) f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫f(x)dx = 1 over the whole range. P(a < X < b) = ∫ab f(x)dx, and P(X = a) = 0 for any single point.
  • Cumulative distribution function (cdf) F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It never decreases, F(−∞) = 0, F(+∞) = 1, and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). For continuous X, f(x) = F′(x).

concepts.title: Expectation and variance
concepts.body:
• Discrete: E(X) = Σ x p(x). Continuous: E(X) = ∫ x f(x)dx.
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; SD = √Var(X).
  • E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). Adding a constant does not change the variance.
  • E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) always.
  • If X and Y are independent: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) and Var(X ± Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) (plus in both cases).

Example: X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities k, 2k, 3k. Then 6k = 1, k = 1/6. E(X) = (0 + 2 + 6)/6 = 4/3. E(X²) = (0 + 2 + 12)/6 = 7/3. Var(X) = 7/3 − 16/9 = 5/9.

concepts.title: Moment generating function
concepts.body:
• MX(t) = E(etX). The r-th raw moment is the r-th derivative of M at t = 0, so M′(0) = E(X).
  • MaX+b(t) = ebt MX(at). For independent X, Y: MX+Y(t) = MX(t) MY(t).

concepts.title: Binomial distribution
concepts.body:
Use when there are n independent trials, each a success (probability p) or failure (q = 1 − p).

  • P(X = r) = nCr pr qn−r, r = 0, 1, …, n.
  • Mean = np, variance = npq, SD = √(npq). Since q < 1, variance < mean.
  • Symmetric when p = ½; positively skewed when p < ½; negatively skewed when p > ½.
  • From mean and variance: q = variance ÷ mean, p = 1 − q, n = mean ÷ p.

Example: n = 10, p = 0.4. Mean = 4, variance = 10 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 2.4.

concepts.title: Poisson distribution
concepts.body:
Counts of rare events in a fixed interval (misprints per page, accidents per day).

  • P(X = r) = e−λ λr / r!, r = 0, 1, 2, …
  • Mean = variance = λ.
  • Limit of binomial when n is large, p is small and np = λ stays fixed.
  • Sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with λ = λ1 + λ2.
  • Recurrence: P(r + 1) = P(r) × λ/(r + 1).
  • Always positively skewed.

Example: λ = 2. P(0) = e−2 ≈ 0.1353, P(1) = 2e−2 ≈ 0.2707, P(2) = 2e−2 ≈ 0.2707.

concepts.title: Normal distribution
concepts.body:
• Bell-shaped, symmetric about μ. Mean = median = mode = μ.
  • Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ; Z has mean 0 and SD 1.
  • Skewness 0; β2 = 3 (mesokurtic). Points of inflexion at μ ± σ. Total area = 1, half on each side of μ.
  • QD ≈ (2/3)σ (more exactly 0.6745σ); MD ≈ (4/5)σ (0.7979σ).
  • Sum of independent normals is normal.

concepts.title: Which distribution to use
concepts.body:
Clue in the questionUse
Fixed n trials, success or failure, constant pBinomial
Rare events, "on average λ per page/hour"Poisson
"First success on the k-th trial"Geometric
"r-th success"Negative binomial
Draws without replacement from a small lotHypergeometric
"Equally likely anywhere between a and b"Uniform
Waiting time, life of a bulb, constant failure rateExponential
Heights, marks, measurement errorsNormal

varieties.name: Probability tables, expectation and variance
varieties.how: First use Σp = 1 to find any unknown k. Then E(X) = Σxp, E(X²) = Σx²p and Var = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

example.q: X takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities k, 2k, 3k. Find Var(X).

varieties.name: Density and distribution functions
varieties.how: Set the total area ∫f(x)dx = 1 to find k; integrate f over the interval for a probability; use ∫x f(x)dx for the mean.

example.q: f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 (and 0 elsewhere) is a pdf. Find k and P(X ≤ 1).

varieties.name: Binomial distribution
varieties.how: Use <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub>p<sup>r</sup>q<sup>n−r</sup>. If mean and variance are given, q = variance/mean, then p and n.

example.q: A binomial distribution has mean 4 and variance 3. Find n and p.

varieties.name: Poisson distribution
varieties.how: Use P(r) = e<sup>−λ</sup>λ<sup>r</sup>/r!. Mean and variance are both λ. For "at most" add the terms.

example.q: Accidents at a crossing follow a Poisson distribution with mean 3 per week. Find P(at most 1 accident in a week). (e<sup>−3</sup> ≈ 0.0498)

varieties.name: Geometric, negative binomial and hypergeometric
varieties.how: Spot the wording: "first success on the k-th try" is geometric, "r-th success" is negative binomial, "without replacement from a lot" is hypergeometric.

example.q: A fair die is thrown until a six appears. Find the probability that the first six comes on the third throw.
steps: Two failures then one success: q<sup>2</sup>p.

varieties.name: Uniform and exponential distributions
varieties.how: Uniform: mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12, probability = length ÷ (b − a). Exponential: mean 1/λ, P(X > x) = e<sup>−λx</sup>.

example.q: The life of a bulb is exponential with mean 2 years. Find the probability it lasts more than 4 years.

varieties.name: Normal distribution
varieties.how: Convert to Z = (X − μ)/σ, sketch the curve, and add or subtract the table areas from 0 to z.

tips: Binomial: variance is less than mean; Poisson: variance equals mean. Use this to identify the distribution from given values.
If a binomial question gives variance greater than mean, it is impossible (q would exceed 1).
For the normal curve, draw a quick sketch and shade the area before adding or subtracting table values.
Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X): the constant b disappears and the sign of a does not matter.
For a continuous variable, P(X < a) and P(X ≤ a) are the same.
Exponential and geometric are the two memoryless distributions.
traps: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X, Y, not the difference.
Mean of the exponential is 1/λ, not λ.
The uniform variance divides by 12, not by 2 or 4.
Check which geometric form is meant: trials until success (mean 1/p) or failures before success (mean q/p).
A pdf value f(x) can be greater than 1; only the total area must equal 1.
